quote: Anyone reporting sudden chest pains should have been hauled off by an ambulance instantly.
content: The model that generated the confusion was false, and the story that "could not have happened" describes a well-documented failure mode. A substantial share of EMS calls end in non-transport, and paramedic judgments that transport is unnecessary miss serious conditions at rates on the order of one in ten (Brown et al. 2009); patients refusing or being released after evaluation for chest pain and later deteriorating is a recognized category (Knight et al. 2003). The narrator's "they'd have hauled him off if there was the tiniest chance" was not a correct model strained by an anomaly. It was an incorrect model that happened, this once, to face a fabricated report. The essay's lesson, trust the confusion, is drawn from a case where the confusion was itself a symptom of ignorance about how ambulances work.

quote: And the Medical Establishment was always right. Every single time.
content: An induction from a handful of personal visits, presented as a fact about medicine. About one in twenty outpatients experience a diagnostic error each year (Singh, Meyer & Thomas 2014), and roughly two percent of patients with acute myocardial infarction presenting to emergency departments are mistakenly sent home, with doubled mortality (Pope et al. 2000). Chest pain is the textbook case of under-triage. The essay's error was not, as it says, excess deference to a correct establishment; it was treating a small personal sample as the establishment's base rate, which is the mistake the sequence elsewhere calls generalizing from too few examples.

quote: It makes you wonder what’s the point of having economists if we’re just going to ignore them.
content: The aside asserts a causal story (mandated treatment drives emergency-department closures) as if it were an economists' consensus. The federal mandate requires screening and stabilization, not treatment, and the closures of 1990-2009 were associated with for-profit ownership, competitive markets, safety-net status and low margins rather than with the mandate as such (Hsia, Kellermann & Shen 2011); uncompensated care is a small fraction of hospital revenue. An essay about noticing when one's model doesn't fit contains, in passing, a confident political-economy model supported by nothing, offered as the obvious view of an expert class that did not hold it.

quote: Alas, belief is easier than disbelief
content: The cited support is Gilbert's "Spinozan" model, on which comprehending a claim entails initially accepting it. Subsequent work found the effect depends on the reader having no relevant knowledge: when background knowledge is available, false statements are rejected as fast as true ones are accepted, with no window of automatic belief (Richter, Schroeder & Wöhrmann 2009), and the neural signature of evaluating statements does not show the asymmetry the model predicts (Hasson, Simmons & Todorov 2005). The narrator did not fail to disbelieve because disbelief is hard; by the essay's own account, he generated a specific rationalization to fit a story into a model he was attached to, which is motivated reasoning, not the Spinozan default.
